📰 Introduction: what a news feed is

Hinglish samajh: News feed ek lagatar badalti hui list hai jisme aapke dosto ya follow kiye hue logon ki posts (status, photos, videos, links) dikhti hain, jaise Facebook ka News Feed, Instagram feed aur Twitter timeline. Chapter ke do flows: feed publishing (post save karna aur dosto ke feed tak pahunchana) aur news feed building (dosto ki posts ko naye se purane order mein jama karna). Poora design inhi dono ko tez aur sasta banane ke bare mein hai.

A news feed is the constantly updating list of stories on your home page: status updates, photos, videos and links posted by the people you follow or are friends with. Facebook's News Feed, Instagram's feed and Twitter's timeline are all examples. It is one of the most common system design questions because it combines almost every topic: databases, caching, queues, fan-out and scaling.

The design question is deceptively simple: "When I open the app, show me the latest posts of my friends." But think about what it means at scale. Millions of people post at the same time, and each post must show up in the feeds of everyone who follows that person. And when you open the app, your feed must appear within a fraction of a second.

The chapter splits the system into two flows. Feed publishing happens when a user posts: the post is saved and delivered to the friends' feeds. News feed building happens when a user opens the app: their feed is assembled from the posts of their friends in reverse chronological order. Almost every decision in this chapter is about how to make these two flows fast and cheap.

✨ Features

  • A constantly updating list of posts from your connections.
  • Examples: Facebook News Feed, Instagram feed, Twitter timeline.
  • Two flows: publishing and building.

✅ Benefits

  • Shows relevant, recent content to each user.
  • Drives engagement with the product.
  • A rich design problem that tests many skills.

⚠️ Problems

  • A single post may need to reach millions of feeds.
  • Reading must be fast even for users with thousands of friends.
  • Storage and cache memory grow quickly.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Introduction

A news feed system displays a constantly updating list of posts (status updates, photos, videos, and links) from a user’s connections. Examples include Facebook’s news feed, Instagram’s feed, and Twitter’s timeline. This chapter explores the design of a scalable news feed system.

Interview questions and answers

What is a news feed system?
A system that shows each user a constantly updating list of posts (text, photos, videos, links) from the people they are connected to.
What are the two main flows?
Feed publishing (store a post and deliver it to friends' feeds) and news feed building (collect friends' posts and show them newest first).
Cross question: Why is it hard?
Because of fan-out: one post must reach many feeds, and reads must be instant even for users with thousands of connections.
Examples of news feeds?
Facebook News Feed, Instagram feed and the Twitter timeline.

📝 Step 1: Requirements and scale

Hinglish samajh: Requirements: web aur mobile dono, post publish karna aur dosto ki posts feed mein dekhna, naye se purane order mein (reverse chronological), ek user ke zyada se zyada 5,000 dost, 10 million daily active users, aur feed mein text, images aur videos. 5,000 dosto ka matlab ek post ko 5,000 feeds tak pahunchana pad sakta hai, jo aage push aur pull ke chunav mein kaam aayega.

Before designing, we agree on what to build. The system supports both web and mobile apps. The two main features are: a user can publish a post, and a user can see posts from their friends in the news feed. For simplicity, the feed is sorted in reverse chronological order, meaning newest first (real systems also rank by relevance, but we keep it simple).

The scale is: a user can have up to 5,000 friends, and there are 10 million daily active users (DAU). Feeds can contain text, images and videos, so storage and delivery of media matter too (a CDN helps).

These numbers matter. 5,000 friends means one post may have to be written into 5,000 feeds. 10 million DAU means millions of people reading their feed every day. The feed must load fast, and a post should appear soon after it is published. Keep these in mind when we compare push and pull models later.

Requirements

RequirementValue
PlatformsWeb and mobile
FeaturesPublish a post; see friends' posts in the feed
SortingReverse chronological order (newest first)
Friends per userUp to 5,000
Traffic10 million daily active users

✨ Features

  • Web and mobile support.
  • Publish posts and read the feed.
  • Reverse chronological ordering for simplicity.

✅ Benefits

  • A focused scope that fits a short interview.
  • Clear scale numbers.
  • Reverse chronological order keeps the ranking simple.

⚠️ Problems

  • Real feeds are ranked, which is much more complex.
  • 5,000 friends makes fan-out expensive.
  • Media increases storage and bandwidth cost.

Interview questions and answers

What are the requirements?
Web and mobile; publish posts and view friends' posts; newest-first ordering; up to 5,000 friends; 10 million DAU; text, images and videos.
Why reverse chronological order?
It simplifies the problem. Ranking by relevance would need a machine learning model and more components.
Cross question: What would change if the feed were ranked?
You would need a ranking service with features and scores, and a way to keep a candidate pool per user, which changes how feeds are stored and read.
Cross question: Why does the friend limit matter?
It bounds the fan-out cost of one post and the number of posts to merge for one read.

🔌 Step 2: The two flows and the APIs

Hinglish samajh: High-level design mein do flows hain. Feed publishing mein post cache aur database mein likhi jaati hai aur dosto ke feeds mein pahunchayi jaati hai. News feed building mein dosto ki posts naye se purane order mein jama hoti hain. Do API: POST /v1/me/feed (content aur auth_token) post karne ke liye, aur GET /v1/me/feed (auth_token) feed padhne ke liye.

The high-level design has two flows. In feed publishing, when a user publishes a post, the data is written to the cache and the database, and the post is populated into the news feeds of friends. In news feed building, the news feed is built by aggregating friends' posts in reverse chronological order. Keeping them separate lets us optimize each independently.

There are two main APIs, both over HTTP. The feed publishing API is POST /v1/me/feed with the parameters content (the text of the post) and auth_token (to authenticate the request). The news feed retrieval API is GET /v1/me/feed with the parameter auth_token. The word me in the path means "the current user, found from the token".

  • News feed building reads and merges posts.

  • The flows can be scaled and tuned separately.
  • The API is tiny and easy to use.
  • The token identifies the user, so the path stays simple.

⚠️ Problems

  • The read path is much busier than the write path.
  • The APIs need authentication and rate limiting.
  • Large feeds need pagination.

The design includes two main flows:

  1. Feed Publishing: A user publishes a post, which is written to the database and propagated to their friends’ feeds.
  2. News Feed Building: A user retrieves their news feed by aggregating posts from friends in reverse chronological order.
  1. Feed Publishing API:
    • Endpoint: POST /v1/me/feed
    • Params: content (post text) and auth_token (authentication).
  2. News Feed Retrieval API:
    • Endpoint: GET /v1/me/feed
    • Params: auth_token (authentication).

Interview questions and answers

What are the two APIs?
POST /v1/me/feed with content and auth_token to publish, and GET /v1/me/feed with auth_token to read the feed.
Why split publishing and building?
Each has different needs: publishing is write-heavy fan-out, and building is a fast read. Splitting lets you optimize each.
Cross question: How would you paginate the feed?
Use a cursor, such as the last post ID seen, and return the next page of older posts, rather than an offset that shifts as new posts arrive.
Cross question: Why authenticate every call?
To know whose feed to build and to stop others from posting or reading in someone else's name.

✍️ The feed publishing flow

Hinglish samajh: Post publish karne par: client API call karta hai, load balancer web servers ko bhejta hai, web servers authenticate aur rate limit karte hain, post service post ko database aur cache mein store karti hai, fanout service use dosto ke news feeds mein push karti hai, aur notification service dosto ko batati hai. User ko fan-out khatam hone ka intezaar nahi karna padta.

Let us follow what happens when a user publishes a post. 1. The user makes the request through the feed publishing API from a web or mobile client. 2. A load balancer distributes the traffic to the web servers. 3. The web servers authenticate the request and enforce rate limits (to stop spam), and then redirect the request to the right services. 4. The post service stores the post in the database and in the cache. 5. The fanout service pushes the new post to the friends' news feeds; the feed data is kept in a cache for fast retrieval. 6. The notification service informs friends that a new post is available (see chapter 10).

Notice that the user does not wait for the whole fan-out to finish. The post is saved first, and delivery to friends happens right after (usually in the background with a queue), so publishing stays fast even for users with many friends.

How it works, step by step

  1. The user publishes a post through the API.
  2. The load balancer sends the request to a web server.
  3. The web server authenticates the user and applies rate limits.
  4. The post service stores the post in the database and the cache.
  5. The fanout service pushes the post to friends' feeds in the cache.
  6. The notification service tells friends about the new post.

✨ Features

  • Post service stores the post.
  • Fanout service delivers it to friends' feeds.
  • Notification service alerts friends.

✅ Benefits

  • The user gets a quick response.
  • Each service does one job.
  • Rate limiting and authentication protect against abuse.

⚠️ Problems

  • Fan-out can be heavy for users with many friends.
  • Notifications can be noisy.
  • Failures between steps need retries.

Interview questions and answers

Describe the feed publishing flow.
The request goes through a load balancer to web servers, which authenticate and rate limit; the post service stores the post; the fanout service pushes it to friends' feeds in the cache; the notification service alerts friends.
Why rate limit publishing?
To prevent spam and abuse that could flood the system and friends' feeds.
Cross question: What if the fanout fails halfway?
The post is already saved, so use a queue with retries; the fan-out job can resume and is idempotent (adding a post ID twice has no extra effect).
Cross question: Why store the post before the fan-out?
So the post is durable even if fan-out is delayed, and so feeds only need to contain the post ID.

📖 The news feed building flow

Hinglish samajh: Feed padhne par: user GET /v1/me/feed bhejta hai, load balancer web server ko deta hai, web server news feed service ko request deta hai, service news feed cache se post IDs laati hai, phir post aur user ki poori details cache ya database se laati hai, aur poora feed client ko lauta deti hai. Feed cache mein sirf post IDs hote hain, isse memory kam lagti hai. Images aur videos CDN se aate hain.

Now the reading side. 1. A user sends a request to retrieve the news feed, for example GET /v1/me/feed. 2. The load balancer redirects the request to a web server. 3. The web servers forward the request to the news feed service. 4. The news feed service fetches the list of post IDs from the news feed cache. 5. To build a complete feed, the service also fetches the full details of each post (user name, profile picture, post content, counts) from the user and post caches or databases. 6. The fully hydrated news feed is returned to the client as JSON for rendering.

Notice a key idea: the feed cache stores only post IDs (a small number per post), not full posts. The detailed content is fetched separately, mostly from other caches. This keeps the feed cache small and fast, and avoids storing a copy of the full post in every follower's feed.

How it works, step by step

  1. The user requests the feed with GET /v1/me/feed.
  2. The load balancer sends the request to a web server.
  3. The web server forwards it to the news feed service.
  4. The service reads the list of post IDs from the news feed cache.
  5. It fetches the full post and user details from the caches or databases.
  6. The complete feed is returned to the client.

✨ Features

  • The feed cache stores post IDs.
  • Post details come from caches or databases.
  • Media is served by a CDN.

✅ Benefits

  • Fast reads: a few cache lookups.
  • The feed cache uses little memory.
  • Post content is stored once, not once per follower.

⚠️ Problems

  • Hydrating many posts needs several lookups.
  • Cache misses fall back to the database.
  • Deleted posts must be removed or skipped.

Describe the news feed building flow.
The service reads post IDs from the news feed cache, fetches full post and user details from caches or databases, and returns the assembled feed to the client.
Why store only post IDs in the feed cache?
To save memory: the content is stored once elsewhere, and each follower's feed just keeps small references.
Cross question: What if a post was deleted?

Cross question: How do images load fast?

📣 Deep dive: fanout on write, fanout on read and the hybrid model

Hinglish samajh: Fan-out matlab nayi post ko saare dosto ke feed tak pahunchana. Fanout on write (push) mein post publish hote hi dosto ke feed mein daal di jaati hai: read tez, par bahut dosto wale user ke liye mehenga aur inactive users ke liye bekaar. Fanout on read (pull) mein feed padhte samay banta hai: inactive users ke liye theek par read dheema. Hybrid model: zyadatar users ke liye push, aur celebrities jaise bahut followers wale users ke liye pull.

Fan-out means delivering a new post to all the friends' feeds. There are two models. Fanout on write (push model): the post is pushed to every friend's feed at the time it is published. The pros: the feed is precomputed in real time, so reading is very fast, and it is fast because the work is done at write time. The cons: if a user has many friends, fetching the friend list and generating the feeds is slow and expensive (the "hotkey" problem), and for inactive users it wastes resources because they may never open the app.

Fanout on read (pull model): the feed is built when the user asks for it. The pros: it works well for inactive users, because nothing is computed until they read, and there is no hotkey problem since nothing is pushed. The cons: reading is slow, because the feed is assembled at request time.

The solution in the notes is a hybrid approach: use the push model for the majority of users (it gives fast reads), and use the pull model for users with very many connections, such as celebrities, so that their posts are fetched at read time instead of being pushed to millions of feeds. Consistent hashing helps to spread the requests and data evenly, which reduces hot spots.

Fanout on write vs fanout on read

PointFanout on write (push)Fanout on read (pull)
When the feed is builtWhen the post is publishedWhen the user opens the feed
Read speedFast (precomputed)Slow (computed on request)
Write costHigh for users with many friendsLow
Inactive usersWasteful: feeds built for nothingEfficient
Hot key problemYes, for celebritiesNo

✨ Features

  • Push (fanout on write): feeds are precomputed.
  • Pull (fanout on read): feeds are built on request.
  • Hybrid: push for most users, pull for very popular ones.

✅ Benefits

  • Fast reads for most users.
  • No giant fan-out for celebrities.
  • Less wasted work for inactive users.

⚠️ Problems

  • The hybrid model is more complex to implement.
  • Deciding the threshold for "celebrity" needs tuning.
  • Merging two sources at read time adds latency.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Feed Publishing Deep Dive

  1. Web Servers:
    • Authenticate users using auth_token.
    • Enforce rate limits to prevent spam.
  2. Fanout Service:
    • Fanout on Write: Push posts to friends’ feeds at write time.
      • Pros: Real-time updates, fast feed retrieval.
      • Cons: Resource-intensive for users with many friends.
    • Fanout on Read: Pull posts at read time.
      • Pros: Efficient for inactive users.
      • Cons: Slower feed retrieval.
    • Hybrid Approach: Use a push model for most users and a pull model for high-connection users (e.g., celebrities).

The fanout service works as following:

  1. Fetch Friend IDs: Retrieve the friend list from a graph database.
  2. Filter Friends from Cache: Access user settings in the cache to exclude certain friends (e.g., muted friends or selective sharing preferences).
  3. Send to Message Queue: Send the filtered friend list along with the new post ID to a message queue for processing.
  4. Fanout Workers: Workers retrieve data from the message queue and update the news feed cache. The cache stores <post_id, user_id> mappings instead of full user and post objects to save memory.
  5. Store in News Feed Cache: Append new post IDs to the friends’ news feed cache. A configurable limit ensures that only recent posts are stored, as most users focus on the latest content, keeping cache memory consumption manageable.

Interview questions and answers

What is the difference between fanout on write and on read?
On write, the post is pushed to friends' feeds at publish time, so reading is fast but writing is expensive. On read, the feed is built when requested, which saves write cost but makes reading slower.
What is the celebrity problem?
A user with millions of followers would cause millions of feed writes for one post, which is slow and wasteful. The hybrid model pulls their posts at read time.
Cross question: Why does push waste resources for inactive users?
Their feeds get updated even though they may never read them.
Cross question: How do you choose the threshold between push and pull?
By measuring follower counts and fan-out cost, and choosing a limit (for example above some tens of thousands of followers) where write cost starts to hurt. It is tuned with real data.

⚙️ Deep dive: how the fanout service works

Hinglish samajh: Fanout service ke kadam: (1) graph database se author ke dosto ki list laao; (2) user cache ki settings se muted friends ya privacy ke hisaab se filter karo; (3) filtered list aur post ID ko message queue mein bhejo; (4) fanout workers queue se padhkar news feed cache update karte hain; (5) cache mein <post_id, user_id> jode rakhte hain aur memory bachane ke liye sirf recent posts rakhte hain.

Let us open the fanout service and see its steps in detail. 1. Fetch friend IDs: get the list of friends of the author from a graph database, which is a good fit for relationships such as friends and followers. 2. Get friends info from the user cache and filter: read user settings from the cache and exclude some friends, for example friends the author has muted, or when the post is shared only with selected friends (privacy settings).

3. Send friends list and post ID to the message queue: the filtered list of friends and the new post ID go to a queue, which spreads the work and protects the system from bursts. 4. Fanout workers take the data from the queue and update the news feed cache. Think of the news feed cache as a mapping table of <post_id, user_id> pairs: whenever a new post is made, it is appended to the news feed of each friend. We store IDs, not full objects, to save memory. 5. Store <post_id, user_id> in the news feed cache: new post IDs are appended to the friends' feeds. To control memory, there is a configurable limit: only recent posts are kept, because most users only care about the latest posts, so the cache miss rate is low.

How it works, step by step

  1. Fetch the friend IDs of the author from the graph database.
  2. Filter the friends using user settings from the cache (muted friends, privacy rules).
  3. Send the filtered friend list and the post ID to the message queue.
  4. Fanout workers read from the queue.
  5. Workers append the post ID to each friend's entry in the news feed cache, keeping only the most recent entries.

A fanout worker (C#, simplified)

public async Task FanOut(long postId, long authorId)
{
    ␀class="nu">0␀
    var friends = await graph.GetFriendIdsAsync(authorId);

    ␀class="nu">1␀
    friends = friends.Where(f => !settings.HasMuted(f, authorId)).ToList();

    ␀class="nu">2␀
    foreach (var batch in friends.Chunk(class="nu">500))
        await queue.PublishAsync(new FanoutJob(postId, batch));
}

␀class="nu">3␀
public async Task Handle(FanoutJob job)
{
    foreach (var userId in job.UserIds)
    {
        await feedCache.PushAsync(userId, job.PostId);     ␀class="nu">4␀
        await feedCache.TrimAsync(userId, maxLength: class="nu">500); ␀class="nu">5␀
    }
}

✨ Features

  • Friends come from a graph database.
  • Settings filter the friend list.
  • Workers write <post_id, user_id> pairs to the feed cache.

✅ Benefits

  • Queues smooth out bursts.
  • Storing only IDs saves memory.
  • Easy to add more workers when fan-out grows.

⚠️ Problems

  • Fan-out for very large audiences is slow.
  • Feed cache limits mean older posts need a database fallback.
  • Filtering needs fresh settings.

Interview questions and answers

Walk me through the fanout service.
Fetch the author's friend IDs from a graph database, filter using user settings from the cache, send the list and post ID to a queue, and let workers append the post ID to each friend's news feed cache, with a size limit.
Why use a message queue in fan-out?
To decouple publishing from the heavy work, absorb bursts and let workers run in parallel.
Why store only IDs in the feed cache?
To save memory, since the post content is stored once in the post cache or database.
Cross question: What happens when a user scrolls beyond the cached posts?
The service reads older posts from the database or builds them on demand, since the cache keeps only recent items.

🗂️ Deep dive: cache architecture and retrieval

Hinglish samajh: News feed system mein cache paanch layers mein baanta hota hai: news feed cache (post IDs), content cache (post details, popular posts hot cache mein), social graph cache (dost aur followers), action cache (likes, replies, shares) aur counter cache (counts). Feed banate samay service in sab se data leti hai aur zyadatar cache hit hote hain, isliye database par load kam rehta hai.

The notes split the cache into five layers, because different data has different access patterns. The news feed cache stores the IDs of the posts in each feed. The content cache stores post data (the popular ones are kept in a "hot" cache to be extra fast). The social graph cache stores relationship data (friends and followers). The action cache stores what users did with posts: liked, replied, shared. The counter cache stores counts such as likes, replies, followers and following.

When the news feed service builds a feed, it reads the post IDs from the news feed cache, then asks the content cache for each post, the social graph cache for author information, the action cache for "did I like this?" and the counter cache for the numbers. Most of these are cache hits, so the database is rarely touched. Splitting the cache this way also lets each layer be sized, expired and monitored on its own.

The five cache layers

LayerWhat it storesWhy separate
News feed cachePost IDs for each user's feedThe core of fast feed reads
Content cachePost content (popular posts in a hot cache)Posts are shared by many feeds
Social graph cacheFriend and follower relationshipsUsed by fan-out and for filtering
Action cacheLikes, replies and shares by usersShows the user's own actions
Counter cacheCounts of likes, replies, followersCounters change very often

✨ Features

  • Five separate cache layers.
  • Hot cache for popular posts.
  • Counters and actions cached separately.

✅ Benefits

  • Very low database load.
  • Each layer can be tuned and scaled independently.
  • Low latency for feed reads.

⚠️ Problems

  • Many caches must be kept consistent with the database.
  • More caches mean more memory and operations.
  • A cache failure can overload the database.

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · News Feed Retrieval Deep Dive

Cache Architecture

The cache is divided into five layers:

  1. News Feed Cache: Stores post IDs for quick retrieval.
  2. Content Cache: Stores post details (popular posts in hot cache).
  3. Social Graph Cache: Stores user relationship data.
  4. Action Cache: Tracks user actions (likes, replies, shares).
  5. Counter Cache: Maintains counts for likes, replies, followers, etc.

Interview questions and answers

What are the cache layers in a news feed system?
News feed cache (post IDs), content cache (post details), social graph cache (relationships), action cache (likes, replies, shares) and counter cache (counts).
Why separate counters from content?
Counters change very often and need different update and expiry behavior than content, which changes rarely.
Cross question: What is a hot cache?
A faster or larger cache for the most popular posts, so that viral content is served from memory.
Cross question: What happens when a cache node fails?
Reads fall back to the database, so cache replication and gradual warm-up matter to avoid overload.

🚀 Key optimizations: scaling, caching, reliability and monitoring

Hinglish samajh: Aakhri optimizations: database ko shard aur replicate karo, web tier ko stateless rakho, cache layers use karo, consistent hashing aur message queues se reliability badhao, aur QPS, latency aur cache hit rate monitor karo. Celebrity ke liye hybrid fan-out zaroori hai, kyunki ek post ke liye karodon feed writes bahut mehenge padte hain (ye example meri taraf se hai).

The chapter ends with general optimizations that apply to almost any system. Scaling the database: use horizontal scaling and sharding to spread data, and read replicas for heavy read traffic. Keep the web tier stateless so that it can scale by adding servers. Caching: keep frequently accessed data in memory and use cache layers to reduce latency and database load. Reliability: consistent hashing spreads requests evenly across servers, and message queues decouple components and buffer traffic. Monitoring: track metrics such as QPS and latency, and watch cache hit rates to adjust the configuration.

Use the table below, together with the worked example, as a revision sheet. The example shows why the hybrid approach matters (these numbers are my own illustration).

Optimizations at a glance

AreaWhat to do
Database scalingHorizontal scaling, sharding and read replicas
Web tierKeep stateless and scale out
CachingCache hot data in several layers
ReliabilityConsistent hashing and message queues
MonitoringTrack QPS, latency and cache hit rate

  • Stateless web tier and layered caches.

  • A system that scales to millions of users.
  • Resilient to bursts and failures.
  • Measurable and tunable.

⚠️ Problems

  • Many layers add operational cost.
  • Cache consistency needs care.
  • Ranking and personalization would add yet more components.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Key Optimizations

Scaling

  1. Database Scaling:
    • Horizontal scaling and sharding.
    • Use of read replicas for high-traffic queries.
  2. Stateless Web Tier: Keep web servers stateless to enable horizontal scaling.

Caching

  1. Store frequently accessed data in memory.
  2. Use cache layers to reduce latency and database load.

Reliability

  1. Consistent Hashing: Distribute requests evenly across servers.
  2. Message Queues: Decouple system components and buffer traffic.

Monitoring

  1. Track key metrics like QPS (queries per second) and latency.
  2. Monitor cache hit rates and adjust configurations accordingly.

Interview questions and answers

Summarize the news feed design in one minute.
Two flows: publishing stores the post and fans it out through a queue to friends' feed caches (push for normal users, pull for celebrities); building reads post IDs from the feed cache and hydrates them from content, graph, action and counter caches. Scale with sharding, replicas, stateless web servers, queues and monitoring.
What would you monitor?
QPS, latency, cache hit rates, queue lengths for fan-out and the time until a post appears in friends' feeds.
Cross question: How would you add ranking?
Add a ranking service that scores candidate posts using signals like recency, affinity and engagement, and store or compute the ranked list per user.
Cross question: How would you handle a viral post?
Serve it from the hot cache and CDN, and avoid fan-out by pulling it at read time if the author has a huge audience.
